client: I've been having a really hard time since my dad passed away a few weeks ago. I can't seem to focus at work at all — I'll be in the middle of something and just completely lose my train of thought, or I'll find myself staring at the screen for an hour without doing anything. There's this weird mix of sadness and anger inside me that I can't really explain, and honestly I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change any of that.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your father — what you're describing, that foggy inability to focus and that confusing blend of sadness and anger, are all deeply human responses to grief, and it makes complete sense that you're feeling this way just weeks after losing him. You don't have to have it all figured out or even believe that talking will help right now; sometimes just giving these feelings a little space is enough to start. I'm curious — when that anger surfaces, do you have any sense of who or what it seems to be directed toward, or does it feel more like a shapeless weight?

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly the anger thing is... it's hard to pin down. Sometimes it feels directed at him, which then makes me feel like a terrible person because he's gone and I can't exactly argue with him now about all the things that were left unsaid. Other times it just kind of sits in my chest like this heavy, formless thing and I don't even know what to do with it.
therapist: Feeling angry at someone you've lost is one of the most common and least talked-about parts of grief, and it doesn't make you a terrible person — it actually speaks to how much the relationship and those unfinished conversations mattered to you. That heaviness in your chest might be the anger and sadness intertwined with all those things that never got said, which can feel so much harder to process because there's no longer an obvious outlet for them. I wonder — if you could have said one of those unsaid things to him, what do you think it might have been?

client: I think... it would have been something like "why didn't you ever just say you were proud of me, just once." That's what sits in my chest the most, I think — this feeling that I spent so long trying to earn something he never actually gave me, and now I never will get it. And saying it out loud just now made it feel more real, which honestly kind of makes me want to take it back.
therapist: What you just said took real courage, and the fact that it feels more real now isn't something to be afraid of — it means you're finally letting yourself acknowledge a pain you've likely been carrying for a very long time. That longing to be told "I'm proud of you" by a parent is one of the most deeply human needs there is, and grieving the fact that it never came is just as real and valid as grieving his passing itself. I'm wondering — do you have any sense, even a small one, of whether he might have felt that pride even if he never found the words to say it?

client: I've thought about that a lot, honestly. Like, maybe he did feel it somewhere, but... I don't know, it almost makes it worse to think about, because if he felt it and still couldn't say it, what does that mean? It just feels like another version of the same thing — me being left to guess, to fill in the blanks, to never actually know.
therapist: That insight is really profound — you've identified something important, that the uncertainty itself has been part of the wound all along, always being left to decode and interpret rather than simply being told. It makes sense that even a hopeful possibility feels painful when what you needed wasn't a maybe, but a clear, unambiguous "I see you." I'm curious — in your life now, are there places or people where you *don't* have to guess, where you feel seen without having to fill in the blanks?

client: Honestly, when I try to think of someone like that, I come up mostly empty, and that itself feels kind of devastating to admit out loud. Maybe my friend Dara sometimes, but even then I catch myself wondering if I'm reading her right, if she actually wants me around or is just being polite. It's like the habit of guessing is so baked into me that I don't even know how to recognize safety when it might actually be there.
therapist: What you just named is such an important insight — that the habit of guessing became a survival skill growing up, but now it follows you even into relationships that might actually be safe, like with Dara. The fact that you can recognize this pattern, even while you're inside it, is genuinely meaningful and is exactly the kind of awareness that can slowly start to shift things. I'm wondering — can you think of one small moment with Dara that, if you tried to look at it without the filter of doubt, might actually be evidence that she genuinely wants you around?

client: I mean... there was this one time she texted me out of nowhere just to say she'd heard a song that reminded her of me. She didn't want anything, wasn't asking for a favor, just thought of me and reached out. But even as I say that, part of me wonders if I'm reading too much into it, or if it was just a casual thing she does with everyone.
therapist: That moment — her reaching out with no agenda, just "I thought of you" — is actually exactly the kind of evidence that's worth holding onto, and your instinct to minimize it is the pattern you just described doing its work in real time. What's striking is that you noticed it, named it, and questioned it all in the same breath, which tells me part of you *wants* to let it count, even if another part is afraid to. What do you think it would feel like, even just for a moment, to let that text mean exactly what it looks like it means?

client: I think it would feel... really nice, actually, for like a split second. But then almost immediately I'd start waiting for the other shoe to drop, like maybe she texted everyone that day and I'm just reading too much into it. It's almost easier to keep it small so I don't end up feeling stupid for letting myself believe someone actually thought about me.
therapist: What you just described - keeping things small to protect yourself from feeling stupid - makes complete sense as a strategy, especially when you grew up in an environment where hoping for something and not getting it was so painful. But I want to gently reflect back what I'm hearing: you've learned to preemptively take away your own good moments before anyone else can, which means the loss happens either way, just by your own hand instead of someone else's. I wonder — what would it cost you, really, to let that one text be real and meant for you, just as an experiment, even knowing the uncertainty doesn't fully go away?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right, that I'm basically doing the damage myself at this point. But letting it be real feels terrifying in a way that's hard to explain, like I'd be setting myself up to fall from a much higher place if it turns out I read it wrong. I guess what it would cost me is that false sense of control I have right now, and I'm not sure I'm ready to give that up even if it's hurting me.
therapist: What you just described - that the control feels false but still feels necessary - is such an honest and courageous thing to recognize, and you don't have to give it up all at once or before you're ready. Healing doesn't ask you to leap from the highest place immediately; it's more like slowly learning to trust the ground one small step at a time. I'm wondering — is there a tiny, low-stakes version of letting something good be real that might feel just manageable enough to try, something where the "fall" wouldn't feel so catastrophic if it didn't work out?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it's that simple... like just pick something small and practice trusting it. But even thinking about what that "small thing" would be makes me anxious, because honestly everything feels connected, like if I let my guard down even a little in one place, it starts unraveling everywhere else. I don't know if that makes sense, but the idea of a "low-stakes" moment doesn't really feel low-stakes to me.
therapist: That makes complete sense, and I want to honor it — if your guard has been the thing holding everything together for a long time, of course loosening it anywhere feels like a structural risk, not a small experiment. What you're describing isn't resistance or stubbornness; it's actually a very logical response to a life where staying vigilant kept you safe. I'm curious — when you imagine that "unraveling" you're afraid of, what does it look like on the other side of it... is it only loss, or is there any part of you that wonders if something else might be on the other side too?

client: Honestly, when I try to imagine the other side... there's this tiny, almost embarrassing flicker of something that might be relief. Like maybe I wouldn't have to work so hard all the time, constantly scanning for what's about to go wrong. But then the fear just swallows it back up, because what if that relief is just me letting my guard down right before everything actually does fall apart.
therapist: That flicker of relief isn't embarrassing at all — it's actually one of the most important things you've said today, because it means some part of you already knows that the vigilance is exhausting, and can imagine, even briefly, what it might feel like to put it down. The fear that relief itself is a trap, that softening is just the moment before the fall, sounds like it's been reinforced so many times that your nervous system learned to treat hope as a warning sign. I'm wondering — can you remember a time, even once, when you let yourself relax a little and the catastrophe you feared didn't actually come?
